items.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think around my era Quinn Wilson and yours truly were the first guys that really had a chance to really study bass... He was my idol. We all wanted to be like Quinn Wilson... We all came from under Major N. Clark Smith.

ctx.x: And he was playing bass lines anyway.

Yeah, he‟s playing bass line anyway so it was quite easy for him to conform. Everything we call “fist in a bass”, everything was in D flat, E flat so all you had to do [laugh] D flat with your fist or E flat with your finger. So they got to survive and do this thing. Now you look in the jazz books, John Lindsay is considered one of the… of course he was. He made a lot of records but they was not academic at all. I think around my era Quinn Wilson and yours truly were the first guys that really had a chance to…
Well you were a violin player.

items.title: 70980_Quinn Wilson oral history interview
items.q: He was -- we were both in the same neighborhood. ... I'm the cause of Milt Hinton being in music. ... gave another friend of mine, lived around the corner from me, violin.

ctx.x: Well, to go back to bass players, after you became established, did you teach other bass players, or other bass players, younger bass players come to you, like Truck or Milt Hinton, and want you to show them something?
Well, I don't know when Milt Hinton started on bass, because he started on the bass shortly after -- seemed like me, after I did. Might have been in the thirties.
